reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC guidelines
clinicalPearls: Cardiac involvement by sarcoidosis produces non-caseating granulomas in the myocardium and conduction system, and may occur with or without overt systemic disease
Classic presentations include unexplained atrioventricular block in a relatively young adult, ventricular arrhythmias, or heart failure
It should be suspected when a young or middle-aged person develops high-grade heart block without another explanation
Basal septal involvement and patchy scarring are typical, and granulomatous infiltration of the conduction system explains the block
Advanced cardiac imaging, particularly cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement and FDG-PET, is central to detecting active inflammation and scar
Endomyocardial biopsy has low sensitivity because involvement is patchy, so a normal biopsy does not exclude the disease
Immunosuppression aims to suppress active granulomatous inflammation, while device therapy addresses conduction disease and arrhythmic risk
Sudden death can result from either ventricular arrhythmia or complete heart block
reference.pathophysiology: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disorder of uncertain cause in which activated T cells and macrophages form non-caseating granulomas. When the heart is involved, granulomatous inflammation infiltrates the myocardium and conduction tissue, followed by patchy fibrosis. Infiltration of the conduction system causes atrioventricular block, while myocardial scarring creates a substrate for re-entrant ventricular arrhythmias and, with extensive involvement, contractile dysfunction and heart failure. Disease activity may fluctuate between active inflammation and fibrotic scar.
additionalDifferentials: Cardiac amyloidosis and other infiltrative diseases
Lyme carditis or other infective causes of heart block
additionalInvestigations: Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement to identify inflammation and scar
FDG-PET to assess active inflammation and guide immunosuppression
12-lead ECG and ambulatory monitoring for conduction abnormalities and arrhythmia
Echocardiography for regional wall abnormalities and ventricular function
Evaluation for extracardiac sarcoidosis and biopsy of accessible involved tissue
Endomyocardial biopsy in selected cases, recognising its limited sensitivity
redFlags: Unexplained high-grade or complete atrioventricular block in a young or middle-aged adult
Sustained ventricular tachycardia or aborted sudden cardiac death
Syncope suggestive of arrhythmia or conduction block
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the extent of myocardial involvement and ventricular function; early recognition and treatment of active inflammation, together with device protection against arrhythmia and block, improve outcomes. Extensive scarring, poor ventricular function, and refractory ventricular arrhythmias portend a worse course, with sudden death an important cause of mortality.
pitfalls: Attributing heart block in a young person to idiopathic conduction disease without considering sarcoid
Excluding the diagnosis on the basis of a negative endomyocardial biopsy
Overlooking cardiac involvement in patients with known systemic sarcoidosis
Treating inflammation without addressing arrhythmic and conduction risk
Failing to reassess disease activity with imaging during immunosuppression
